# Tree thinking and $f$ statistics




## Theme of this chapter

In this chapter, we will delve a little bit into thinking about demographic
histories (and about statistics we use to study those histories) through the
lens of "tree thinking"---i.e., thinking in terms of genealogies recorded along
the genome and, in particular, the branches in those genealogies. This fits the
context of our work until this point quite naturally, particularly given the
fact that the core component of _slendr_ simulations is a tree sequence.

In the process, we will also change pace a bit, and use _slendr_ as a sort of an
"interactive popgen calculator" to quickly gain insights into population genetic
statistics and explore them them in an interactive way. Our main focus here will
be on $f$-statistics and their interpretation through tracing paths along
trees---particularly the $f_4$ statistic---because they form such a crucial
component of population genomics research.






## Literature

- If you want to know much more technical background into $f_3$ statistics
(introduced in this chapter), and $f_4$ statistics and admixture proportion
estimators $f_4$-ratio (introduced in the following chapter), you can take a
look at the following papers: [Peter,
2016](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/202/4/1485/5930214), [Lipson
2020](https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/doi/abs/10.1111/1755-0998.13230), and
[Patterson _et al._,
2008](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/192/3/1065/5935193).

- There are a number of software tools that can compute $f_3$ statistics on real
data. If you'd like to compare simulated $f$ statistics to empirical results,
take a look at [ADMIXTOOLS 2](https://uqrmaie1.github.io/admixtools/index.html)
or my own R package [_admixr_](https://bodkan.net/admixr).




## Exercise: "Outgroup" $f_3$ as a measure of overlap of tree paths

To ease into the problem of interpreting $f$-statistics as measures of
overlapping paths in "population trees" or---when admixture comes into the
picture---in "admixture graphs", let's briefly return to our familiar $f_3$
statistic.

**Restart your R session, then create a new script `f_null.R` and paste the
following code into that script. As always, read through the code, try to build
a mental model of what it's going to do, then run it and compare your
understanding with the generated visualization of the model.**

(I know this is easy, but being able to read code quickly and efficiently is
the best way to learn to spot bugs.)

```{r}
#| output: false
#| collapse: true
library(slendr)
init_env()

# build a basic population tree structure
p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
px <- population("px", time = 500, N = 1000, parent = p2)

# compile the model and define recording of individuals
model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4, px), generation_time = 1)
schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 5))

# plot the model to check its correctness visually
plot_model(model, schedule = schedule)

# simulate 10 Mb of genomic data for later exploration
ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
```

---

Now, consider the model implemented in our script `f_null.R`, visualized below:

```{r}
#| echo: false
plot_model(model, schedule = schedule)
```

We know from [the paper describing the theory of
$f$-statistics](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/202/4/1485/5930214)
that:

1. **$f_2(A, B)$ statistic measures the branch length between A and B (two
individuals, two groups of individuals, two populations, etc.)**, and similarly

2. **$f_3(C; A, B)$ statistic is defined as the branch length which connects the
internal most recent common ancestor node of A and B with the lineage C**,

3. **$f_4$ (which we will discuss later) has a similar interpretation**.

(These three ideas can be seen graphically in [Figure
1](https://academic.oup.com/view-large/figure/379128872/1485fig1.jpeg) of that
linked paper.)

Another thing established in the paper is the fact that **any $f$-statistic can
be expressed as a linear combination of multiple $f_2$ statistics**. If you're
not familiar with linear algebra, this might sound a bit obscure, but the idea
is simple. More concretely, **for instance, equation (20b) in the same paper
states the following, which decomposes an $f_3$ statistic into a composite of
simpler $f_2$ statistics** (this is what "linear combination" basically is):

$$f_3(A; B, C) = \frac{1}{2} (f_2(A, C) + f_2(A, B) - f_2(B, C))$$

---

**Draw a sketch of the population model (of populations p1, p2, p3, etc.) on a
piece of paper, then trace by hand the paths indicated by the three $f_2$
statistics in this equation on that drawning (again, knowing that $f_2(A, B)$
describes the branch between some two nodes $A$ and $B$. When you "add" and
"subtract" paths based on the equation (graphically by hand!), do you arrive at
the definition of "outgroup" $f_3$ as branch length from A and B towards the
outgroup, as we described it in point 2. above?**


---

When I was writing this chapter, I made a mistake in the equation above, which I
discovered after I wrote a quick simulation to double-check that the equation is
correct. Let's retrace my steps here because it shows why even very quick
simulations can be really useful (almost like a "popgen calculator"!).

**Let's move to R. Use the function `ts_f2()` to implement this equation in
code, computing a "homemade" $f_3(A = p4; B = p1, C = p2)$ statistic which you
just solved on paper, and compare it to the result you get if you run the
computation using the `ts_f3()` function by _slendr_. Do you get the same result
using both methods, and therefore verifying that the equation is correct?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

First let's get our groups of individuals in the tree sequence so that we can
refer to populations more easily:

```{r}
s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
s
```

Let's compose a "homemade" $f_3$ statistic as a linear combination of $f_2$
statistics as given by the equation:

```{r}
homemade_f3 <- 1/2 * (
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"])$f2 +
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p2"])$f2 -
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p1"], B = s["p2"])$f2
)
homemade_f3
```

Finally, let's compute $f_3$ using the "official" built-in _slendr_ function:

```{r}
simulated_f3 <- ts_f3(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"], C = s["p2"])
simulated_f3
```

You can see that the `ts_f3()` implementation gives basically the same value as
our "homemade" implementation based on a linear combination of $f_2$
statistics, just as predicted by the underlying math!

:::









## Exercise: Mutations versus branches

Do you recall how I told you that you don't have to add mutations to your tree
sequence `ts`, and still be able to compute population genetic statistics? But
that you can safely add them with `ts_mutate()` anyway?

The reason this works is because some very smart people figured out a
mathematical [duality between mutation-based and branch-based
statistics](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/215/3/779/5930459)---it
actually doesn't matter which way we compute our statistics, they give
mathematically the same result in terms of theoretical statistical expectations
(i.e., expectations of what happen in real data).

---

**Repeat the previous exercise, but this time specify `mode = "branch"` in all
your `ts_f3()` and `ts_f2()` commands.** I suggest that you make a copy of your
`ts_f3()` and `ts_f2()`-based code in your `f_null.R` script and and modify the
copies for easier comparison. **What numbers do you get compared to the results
of the previous exercise in terms of their scale? Can you relate those values to
what your population tree model visualization indicates (in terms of branch
lenghts)? Look at your sketch with pen and paper again if this helps in putting
your results in clearer context (particularly with regards to split times).**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here are the two code chunks from the previous solution computed by setting
`mode = "branch"`:

```{r}
ts_f3(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"], C = s["p2"], mode = "branch")
```

```{r}
homemade_f3 <- (
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p1"], mode = "branch")$f2 +
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p4"], B = s["p2"], mode = "branch")$f2 -
  ts_f2(ts, A = s["p1"], B = s["p2"], mode = "branch")$f2
) / 2

homemade_f3
```

We can see that when we specify `mode = "branch"`, the returned values of $f$
statistics correspond to the _real branch lengths_ in terms of times in
generations! To see this, just take a look at your model sketch again, counting
how much time there's between split times. This is quite cool because as we
discussed, the mathematical expectation of $f_3$ statistic does, in fact,
represent the overlap of paths in a tree going from p1 and p2 to the outgroup
p4:

```{r}
#| echo: false
plot_model(model)
```

:::


Hopefully, you can now appreciate that there's nothing magical about $f$
statistics. Even though their practical interpretation can get sometimes
complicated, internally they _always_ boil down to tracing paths through
population trees in order to obtain statistical expectations of allele frequency
correlations between lineages under study, easily visualized by tracing paths
through population trees.

In a way, setting `mode = "branch"` can be understood as instructing _slendr_ to
compute the results --- in this case, of the $f_3$ statistic --- in "real time
units" (in the case of this simple model, in generations).











## Exercise: Basic intuition into the $f_4$ statistic

Now let's finally dig into exploring the most critical component of population
genetics research (particularly in the context of ancient DNA)---the venerable
$f_4$-statistic, [formally
established](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/192/3/1065/5935193) by
Nick Patterson and David Reich in 2012.

From the [intuitive follow-up paper on $f$-statistics by Benjamin
Peter](https://academic.oup.com/genetics/article/202/4/1485/5930214), we know
that (in a very similar way to $f_2$ and $f_3$) **the $f_4(W, X; Y, Z)$
statistic can be interpreted as the overlap between the paths in a tree
connecting the pairs W-X and Y-Z**, as is demonstrated in [Figure
1](https://academic.oup.com/view-large/figure/379128872/1485fig1.jpeg) of the
linked paper.

That said, **what value does any given $f_4$ statistic _actually_ gives you
depends on the (in practice, hidden) underlying demographic model which
determines how populations are related**---this is what we need to infer---**and
also what individuals assign into each of the four positions of the $f_4$
"quartet configuration"**.

---

**Knowing the relationships between populations encoded by the tree model
programmed in your script `f_null.R` and the interpretation of the $f_4$
statistic, what is the expected value of $f_4(p1, px; p3, p4)$ for this model?
Try to answer by taking a look at the sketch of your model and tracing the path
overlaps between p1-px and p3-p4 pairs, then compute the statistic on a `ts`
simulated data with the `ts_f4()` function to verify your intuition. Does your
simulation give you the _exact_ result you might expect based on the
visualization of the model alone? If it doesn't give you the _exact_ expected
result, why could this be?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### click to see the solution

As we can see below, $f$-statistics theory tells us that the value should be
zero, but without having a reference baseline, we get a number which is very
tiny (the value in the `f4` column). But how tiny would it have to be to be
"basically zero"?

```{r}
ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])
```

The reason we didn't get _exactly_ zero is stochastic noise of any evolutionary
process, which means that that along a genome (even a small one, only 10 Mb of
simulated sequence) there are many possible trees. Sometimes, [incomplete
lineage sorting](https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Incomplete_lineage_sorting) will
lead to genealogical trees which do not fit the expected "well-behaved"
population tree like the one we see when we run `plot_model()`. We will see
examples of this at the end of this chapter.

That said, gene trees that don't fit the overall population trees will tend to
"average out", particularly when we look across many different regions of the
genome---this is why the simulated $f_4$ gets very close to zero in practice.

:::

---

As suggested in the solution above, the reason we don't get a perfectly zero
expected value of the $f_4$ is because of ILS and stochasticity. Let's test
this hypothesis now.

**First, evaluate `ts` in your R console and note how many trees do you have in
your 10 Mb tree-sequence.**

**Now, restart your R session (`Session -> Restart R`). Then, temporarily change
the `N` of all populations in your model to 1 and re-run your script to get a
new `ts` and compute the same $f_4$ statistic again. $N_e$ of one implies a
ludicrously high amount of drift, which should eliminate ILS completely, giving
us $f_4$ close to its mathematical expectation of zero. Is this true in your new
simulation? And how many trees does your tree sequence have with this high
amount of drift?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

```{r}
#| echo: false
ts_num_trees <- ts$num_trees
```

We changed all N sizes to 1, then we rerun the entire script `f_statistics.R`
again:

```{r}
library(slendr)
init_env()

# !!!
# note the temporary change to N = 1
# !!!
p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1, parent = p2)
px <- population("px", time = 500, N = 1, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4, px), generation_time = 1)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 5))

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
```

Now let's compute the $f_4$ again on the `ts` tree sequence produced by this
extreme model. When we do this, we see that the value really is zero, exactly as
the theory predicts:

```{r}
ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])
```

Indeed, when we type `ts` into the R console, we see that it only contains
`{r} ts$num_trees`
individual trees compared to the previous count of
`{r} ts_num_trees`,
consistent with an absolutely extreme amounts of genetic drift in your model:

```{r}
ts
```


:::

---

Of course, changing $N_e$ to value of 1 as we did above is a drastic measure of
only theoretical utility. We could hardly get away with doing that, if we wanted
to use simulations to make a point in our research paper.

How do we deal with the unavoidable stochasticity in our simulations then? This
wasn't much of a problem in exercises in the previous chapters, but we need the
way to solve this to be able to get useful, applicable results.

Let's look into this now.

```{r}
#| echo: false
p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
px <- population("px", time = 500, N = 1000, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4, px), generation_time = 1)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 5))

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
```





## Exercise: Reducing stochastic noise via simulation replicates

**First, set the `N` sizes of your populations in your model from 1 back to
1000, then re-run your script to make sure the original `model` is compiled.**

As a means to tame the stochasticity and help meaningful statistical patterns
stand out, I recently implemented a new _slendr_ function `ts_replicates()`,
specifically for this workshop! The way it works is like this:

```{r}
#| eval: false
ts_replicate(
  n = <number of replicates to simulate>,
  {
    # ...
    # a block of slendr code wrapped in { ... } containing a ts simulation
    # and a statistical computation we want to run in given replicates
    # ...
  }
)
```

---

**Take a look at its manual page under `?ts_replicates`, then use it to run 10
replicate simulations of the $f_4$ statistic above** (the one which should give
us exactly zero value, but didn't), **saving the result to variable `df`. What
format does the result have? When you visualize the distribution of $f_4$ values
across all 10 replicates, are they more interpretable in terms of the
statistical expectation for this particular $f_4$ quartet?**

::: aside

**Note:** If you want to speed up the replicate simulation, note that
`?ts_replicate` allows running multiple simulations in parallel.

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's how we can modify the "template" above to answer this question:

```{r}
df <- ts_replicate(

  # run 10 replicates ...
  n = 10,

  # ... of the following block of code...
  {

  # ... which first simulates a tree sequence ...
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  # ... and then computes a data frame with the given f4 statistic ...
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
  ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"])

  } # ... the function automatically binds all data frames into single one
)

```

We can see that we get the same format of the data frame as normally produced by
the `ts_f4()` function, except with a new column `rep` added, indicating a
replicate number.

```{r}
df
```

This means we can visualize their distribution easily like this, for example:

```{r}
library(ggplot2)

ggplot(df, aes(statistic, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed")
```

As we can see, when we run multiple replicates of the simulation, we are able to
"control" the stochastic noise a bit, making the expected pattern stand out more
clearly: we see that the expected value of `{r} unique(df$statistic)` is really
zero (up to that unavoidable stochastic noise shown by the scatter of individual
replicate values around zero).

:::







## Exercise: Other $f_4$ "quartets"

Of course, $f_4(p1, px; p3, p4)$ is only one possible "quartet configuration".

**Expand your 10 replicates simulation $f_4(p1, px; p3, p4)$ by adding the
computation of $f_4(p1, p3; px, p4)$ and $f_4(p1, p4; px, p3)$ in the same `{
... }` block provided to `ts_replicate()` (making sure you `rbind()` all three
data resulting frames together at the end).**

**How would you compare the interpretation of the three $f_4$ statistics? Again,
use sketching of paths on a population tree on paper to try to figure it out
first based on the definition of what $f_4$ between the given two pairs of
lineages indicate, then compare your understanding to what you see when you
visualize the distributions of those three statistics.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Let's add the computation of all three $f_4$ statistics in the same replicate
simulation pipeline:

```{r}
df <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  # instead of computing one f4 like before, we compute all three and then
  # bind the three data frames into a single one
  rbind(
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"]), # 1st f4
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p4"]), # 2nd f4
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p3"])  # 3rd f4
  )
})
```

Again, we get a data frame with multiple replicates for each of the three
statistics:

```{r}
df
```

From the mathematical definition of $f_4$ as internal branch lengths between two
pairs of lineages in a given "quartet" and knowing the topological structure of
our population tree, we can predict that the first $f_4$ is expected to be zero
(which is what we established earlier), and the other two $f_4$ statistics are
expected to have the same value representing the internal branch length
connecting two pairs in the "quartet".

This is exactly what we see in our results:

```{r}
ggplot(df, aes(statistic, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed")
```

:::

---

**Make a copy of your `ts_replicate()` code computing the three $f_4$ statistics
and modify it by setting `mode = "branch"`, as we did before, perhaps changing
`df` to `df_branch` in this copied code for easier comparison. Recall that `mode
= "branch"` instructs _slendr_'s internal statistical machinery to use "model
time units" (here, generations) in computing the results based on branches,
instead of mutations. When you visualize the three $f_4$ statistics computed in
this way, do you see this being reflected in the scale (and meaning) of the
numbers which you get back?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Let's save the result in a new data frame `df_branch`:

```{r}
df_branch <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  rbind(
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"), # 1st f4
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"), # 2nd f4
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p3"], mode = "branch")  # 3rd f4
  )
})
```

When we visualize the results, we do indeed see that the `f4` column contains
the expected branch lengths expressed in real generation times! Here are the
results plotted alongside the model using the package _cowplot_ so that the
branch length times can be read more easily:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 10
library(cowplot) # get access to the plot_grid() function

plot_grid(
  # first panel:
  plot_model(model),

  # second panel:
  ggplot(df_branch, aes(statistic, f4)) +
    geom_boxplot() +
    geom_jitter() +
    geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed"),

  # plot both panels in two rows:
  nrow = 2
)
```

:::










## Catching up

This was a lot of work! If you want to check in with the state of our
$f$-statistics exploratory simulation script `f_null.R`, here it is in the form
which showcases the most important results from this chapter so far:

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the entire script

```{r}
#| output: false
##################################################
# load the necessary packages

library(ggplot2)
library(cowplot)

library(slendr)
init_env()

##################################################
# define the basic structure of our demographic model

p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
px <- population("px", time = 500, N = 1000, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4, px), generation_time = 1)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 5))

##################################################
# simulate replicates of the three f4 statistics
# (based on branches)

df <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  rbind(
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p2"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p3"], mode = "branch")
  )
})

##################################################
# visualize branch-based f4 statistics alongside
# the corresponding demographic model (note that
# ggplot figures can be stored in variables!)

p_model <- plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)

p_df <- ggplot(df, aes(statistic, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed")

p_panels <- plot_grid(p_model, p_df, nrow = 2)

p_panels
```

:::











## Exercise: Interpreting $f_4$ as an admixture hypothesis test

Admittedly, thinking about $f$ statistics as measures of allele frequency
correlations between populations and interpreting them as overlapping branch
lengths is intellectually interesting in terms of population genetics theory,
but in practice, they are most famous (and most famously used) as admixture
tests.

**Create a new script `f_admixture.R` and copy my solutions to the exercises in
this chapter available under the _"Catching up"_ section above into that
script.** This is just to get the same starting point. **Restart your R session
(`Session -> Restart R`) then skim through this script and re-run it. Having
gone through the exercises, the code should look somewhat familiar and the
visualization you obtain by typing out `p_panels` into your R console (the
branch lengths encoded by the three $f_4$ statistics we studied) should make
sense.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's the final visualization of the three $f_3$ statistics for easier
reference as you work on the following exercise.

```{r}
#| fig-height: 10
#| echo: false
p_panels
```

:::


---

Right now our script `f_admixture.R` doesn't have any admixture. It still
contains what we established in this chapter so far: a statistical null model of
"nothing interesting happened in the demographic history in terms of potential
admixture", as is reflected in the $f_4$ values we obtained.

**Introduce the following two changes to the `f_admixture.R` script to turn it
into an admixture model:**

1. **Program a `gene_flow()` event `gf`, introducing 20% gene-flow from `p3` to
`px` between 400 and 300 generations ago.**

2. **Add this `gf` event into the `model` compilation step executed by
`compile_model()`.**

**With the steps 1. and 2. done, your model now includes admixture. Re-run the
script again, and inspect the final visualization obtained by typing out
`p_panels` into your R console. You should see an admixture edge added to your
population tree.**

---

**How does admixture from `p3` to `px` affect the branch lengths compared to the
previous model `f_null.R` when you visualize the replicates for each of the
three $f_4$ statistics from the admixture model? Pay particular attention to the
$f_4(p1,px;p3,p4)$ statistic which had an expected value of zero before---does
it still have a zero value? If not, why, and what does it tell us about it
utility to study admixture histories?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's only the final visualization of the figure in the `p_panel` variable:

```{r}
#| fig-height: 10
#| echo: false
##################################################
# load the necessary packages

library(ggplot2)
library(cowplot)

library(slendr)
init_env()

##################################################
# define the basic structure of our demographic model

p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)
px <- population("px", time = 500, N = 1000, parent = p2)

gf <- gene_flow(from = p3, to = px, start = 400, end = 300, proportion = 0.2)

model <- compile_model(
  populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4, px),
  gene_flow = gf,
  generation_time = 1
)

schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 10))

##################################################
# simulate replicates of the three f4 statistics
# (based on branches)

df <- ts_replicate(
  n = 10, {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)
  
  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)

  rbind(
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p4"], mode = "branch"),
    ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p3"], mode = "branch")
  )
})

##################################################
# visualize branch-based f4 statistics alongside
# the corresponding demographic model (note that
# ggplot figures can be stored in variables!)

p_model <- plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)

p_df <- ggplot(df, aes(statistic, f4)) +
  geom_boxplot() +
  geom_jitter() +
  geom_hline(yintercept = 0, color = "red", linetype = "dashed")

p_panels <- plot_grid(p_model, p_df, nrow = 2)

p_panels
```

As we can see, because of the admixture event, our previously tree-like
population model is no longer tree. In the tree model without an admixture edge,
there was no path overlap between the pairs `p1`-`px` and `p3`-`p4`, which is
why the $f_4(p1,px;p3,p4)$ statistic was zero.

Admixture is a violation of "treeness", because "mathematical" trees are not
allowed to have edges (they effectively create "loops" in the
trees)---structures which do have edges are instead called "admixture graphs".
This is why the statistic now significantly deviates from zero (and is
negative).

This is exactly why $f_4$ is useful as a statistical hypothesis test of
admixture---if a population quartet is from a truly tree-like model, this
statistic will always necessarily be zero; conversely, it can only ever be
non-zero if the underlying model (usually hidden, in real-world applications)
involves admixture which violates "treeness".

:::

This is exactly why $f_4$ is useful as a statistical hypothesis test of
admixture---if a population quartet is from a truly tree-like model, this
statistic will always necessarily be zero; conversely, it can only ever be
non-zero if the underlying model involves admixture which violates "treeness".






## Exercise: Estimating admixture proportions

From the little simulation and tree-doodling experiments, we now have a sense of
how $f$ statistics mathematically quantify allele frequency correlations between
lineages of population trees and how they can be interpreted as the amounts of
overlaps of paths traced along branches of those trees.

We also have an idea how different patterns emerge in $f_4$ statistic
expectations when gene-flow is introduced into population trees, adding
admixture edges to them and turning them into so-called "admixture graphs".

It turns out that the same principles allow us to not just test the hypothesis
of whether an admixture event happened in the history of our samples, but also
estimate the proportion of ancestry derived from this admixture---a concept
known as $f_4$-ratio statistics.

---

The theory of $f_4$-ratios can get quite complex, but let's try to get an idea
about its internal workings using a very simple example and build up from there.
We'll end up inventing the $f_4$-ratio statistic from scratch!

**Let's consider our model again and set a goal to estimate how much ancestry of
`px` came from `p3` (or how much came from `p2` into `px`---these are
complementary, of course). Imagine tracing a path through the population from
`px` to `p2` through the tree. Draw a fresh sketch of our five-population model
on paper, and trace this `px`-`p2` path on it.**

**How many such paths can we take through the tree?**

```{r}
#| echo: false
plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)
```

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

There are two paths:

1. We could either go from `px` "to the right" and walk through the tree through
the `p3` population and them "loop over" into the `p2` population.

2. Alternatively, we could go "to the left" and arrive to `p2` "directly"
through the population split of `px` from `p2`.

We only have those two possibilities, because we know that the genetic ancestry
of `px` is effectively derived from admixture between `p2` and `p3` lineages.

(In fact, because this is a simulation, we even know that 20% of the genome of
`px` comes from `p3` and 80% comes from `p2`, meaning that 20% of our paths will
go through the `p3` lineage.)

:::

---

**How many `px` to `p2` paths would we have available if there wasn't any
admixture in the model?**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

If our model didn't have an admixture edge it would be a simple tree, meaning
that we could only trace one path from `px` to `p2` "directly" through the
population split of `px` from `p2`.

:::

---

**Now that we've established the two possible paths from `px` to `p2` in our
population tree, what would be the interpretation of $f_4(p1,p4;px,p2)$ at any
given locus of the genome? What would be the possible values of this $f_4$ in
this situation? Again, try to use pen and paper to figure it out based on the
knowledge of $f_4$ as a measures of internal branches in a tree.**

**Hint:** Remember that we've established that there are two possible paths from
`px` to `p2` in the tree, depending on whether `px` has a genetic ancestry
coming from `p2` or `p3` at a given locus of the genome.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

The $f_4$ statistic in question could give two possible results, depending on
the paths 1. or 2. taken (as explain in the previous section):

1. In the first potential path, $f_4(p1,p4;px,p2)$ would be the length of the
shared internal branch in the tree between pairs `p1`-`p4` and `p2-px` (or,
effectively, `p2`-`p3`, because that locus in `px` originated in `p3` due to
admixture).

2. In the second potential path, $f_4(p1,p4;px,p2)$ would be zero! This is
because in such a situation, there's no overlap between pairs `p1`-`p4` and
`p2`-`p3` in the tree---and so there's no such internal branch.

:::

---

Now for the final punchline!

You've already established that one of the two interpretations of
$f_4(p1,p4;px,p2)$ describes the internal branch in the tree separating the
pairs `p1`-`p4` and `px`-`p2`, which exists for the parts of the genome which
`px` inherited from `p3` (the other interpretation giving a value of zero, by
definition).

**What is the interpretation of $f_4(p1,p4;p3,p2)$? Again, sketch the internal
path represented by this $f_4$ statistic in your tree model on paper.**

---

**Finally, what happens if you would take the value produced by
$f_4(p1,p4;px,p2)$ and divided it by $f_4(p1,p4;p3,p2)$, i.e. what is the
interpretation of the following equation?**

$$\frac{f_4(p1,p4;px,p2)}{f_4(p1,p4;p3,p2)}$$

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

As we've shown in the first part of this exercise, if we want to model the
ancestry of `px` as an admixture of $\alpha$ proportion from `p3` and $(1 -
\alpha)$ proportion from `p2`, we can effectively decompose $f_4(p1,p4;px,p2)$
into two possible outcomes corresponding two two possible quantities:

- one of them is zero (and happens in $(1 - \alpha)$ proportion of cases),

- the other one gives the internal branch length (and happens in $\alpha$
proportion of cases).

We can then use this fact to expand the ratio given in the equation above like
this (using the fact that the red-highlighted branch length is zero, leaving the
rest of the fraction to cancel each other):

$$
\frac{f_4(p1,p4;px,p2)}{f_4(p1,p4;p3,p2)} =
\frac{(1 - \alpha) f_4(p1,p4;p2,p2) + \alpha f_4(p1,p4;p3,p2)}{f_4(p1,p4;p3,p2)} = 
\frac{\textcolor{red}{\cancelto{0}{(1-\alpha)f_4(p1,p4;p2,p2)}} + \alpha \cancel{f_4(p1,p4;p3,p2)}}{\cancel{f_4(p1,p4;p3,p2)}} =
\alpha
$$

And hurray, just like this, we invented the famous $f_4$-ratio estimator for
ancestry proportion!

:::

---

There's one thing to be smart and logical, there's one thing to be able to
derive an equation (or be handed one equation from a paper or a textbook).
Trusting and understanding the equation is another matter---that's when
simulations can be very useful again.

**Use the equation for the $f_4$-ratio estimator of ancestry proportion to write
a new code chunk in your `f_admixture.R` script which will simulate the values
of this estimator expected from our admixture model using a ratio two individual
`ts_f4()` statistics, specifying the quartet configuration accordingly. Then
visualize the admixture proportion thus computed---did your estimator recover
the known value of 20% of admixture?**

**If you want an extra challenge, it turns out there are multiple variations of
how the ancestry proportion can be estimated. Try to find them, add them to your
`ts_replicate()` code and compare them to one another!**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

I managed to come up with three possible $f_4$-ratio variations, all three
programmed and benchmarked below:

- Variant number 1 is the one we derived together, based on tracing the path
from `px` to `p2` through population `p3` (this is predicted to estimate 20%
ancestry).

- Variant number 2 is the complement to the first variant which traces the
ancestry from `px` to `p3` through population `p2` (and therefore is expected to
estimate 80% ancestry).

- Variant number 3 is a little strange and I came up with it by accident when I
was developing the very first $f_4$ ratio exercise. Notice that although it does
produce the correct 20% expectation, it shows a much higher variance (i.e., much
more statistical noise).

```{r}
#| fig-height: 10
props <- ts_replicate(
  n = 50,
  {
  ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 10e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

  s <- ts_names(ts, split = TRUE)
    
  # variant #1 -- this is the variant we derived together
  num1 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p2"])$f4
  den1 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p2"])$f4
  prop1 <- num1 / den1
  
  # variant #2
  num2 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["px"], Z = s["p3"])$f4
  den2 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p3"])$f4
  prop2 <- num2 / den2

  # variant #3 (a weird one?)
  num3 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"])$f4
  den3 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"])$f4
  prop3 <- - num3 / den3
    
  # create a data frame with different variants
  data.frame(
    proportion = c("variant1", "variant2", "variant3 (weird one?)"),
    value = c(prop1, prop2, prop3)
  )
  },
  parallel = parallel::detectCores() - 1
)

p_model <- plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)

p_f4ratios <- ggplot(props, aes(value, color = proportion)) +
    geom_density() +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.2, 0.8), linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
    coord_cartesian(xlim = c(0, 1)) +
    labs(title = "Simulation-based validation of f4-ratio ancestry estimates",
         subtitle = "(three different variations of f4-ratios are shown)",
         x = "ancestry proportion") +
    theme(legend.position = "bottom")

p_ratios <- plot_grid(p_model, p_f4ratios, nrow = 2)

p_ratios
```

**Note that there's still a lot of variance and noise. In a practical setting,
we would run many more simulation replicates (100 or even more) for genomes much
longer than just 10 Mb (for instance, even 100 Mb). We don't do this here
because those simulations would take too long to do on a normal laptop.**

:::

## Catching up

This was even more work! And no wonder---a simulation-based analysis like this
one could easily be part of a real research paper. In fact, many studies which
introduced these theoretical concepts used these simulations as
proof-of-principle, and increasing number of applications include them for
benchmarking and validation of results. Now you know how to do these things as
well!

If you want to check in with the state of the final `f_admixture.R` script,
you can find it below.

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}

```{r}
#| output: false
##################################################
# load the necessary packages

##################################################
# define the basic structure of our demographic model

  # variant #1 -- this is the variant we derived together

  den1 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p3"], Z = s["p2"])$f4

  # variant #2

  den2 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p4"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p3"])$f4
  prop2 <- num2 / den2

  # variant #3 (a weird one?)
  num3 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["px"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"])$f4
  den3 <- ts_f4(ts, W = s["p1"], X = s["p3"], Y = s["p2"], Z = s["p4"])$f4
  prop3 <- - num3 / den3
    
  # create a data frame with different variants
  data.frame(
    proportion = c("variant1", "variant2", "variant3 (weird one?)"),
    value = c(prop1, prop2, prop3)
  )
  },
  parallel = parallel::detectCores() - 1
)

p_model <- plot_model(model, proportions = TRUE)

p_f4ratios <- ggplot(props, aes(value, color = proportion)) +
    geom_density() +
    geom_vline(xintercept = c(0.2, 0.8), linetype = "dashed", color = "red") +
```

## Exercise: What are tree sequences?

We've mentioned the concept of "tree sequence" only in passing so far, although
they've been absolutely central to every single one of our simulations because
of that mysterious `ts` object. However, we've been referring to trees,
genealogies, population trees, etc. throughout the exercises, particularly in
this chapter, although we've never actually looked at those underlying trees at
all.

Generally speaking, for most of the practical work, we don't need to be aware of
the underlying tree-sequence data that much, but it's always a good idea to know
what's going on behind the scenes of the methods that we use, so let's take a
small peek at what actually _is_ hiding behind our familiar `ts` objects. **This
section will be more like a demonstration rather than a "serious exercise", just
in case you're curious about this topic.**


---

**When you type `ts` into your R console, you'll get a summary of the most
important characteristics in your data. For instance, consider a small 100 kb
tree-sequence simulation like this, and note the number of trees (in this case,
`{r} ts$num_trees`), the number of edges, nodes, and mutations:**

```{r}
schedule <- schedule_recording(model, times = 0, list("each", 1))

ts <-
    msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8, schedule = schedule, random_seed = 42) %>%
    ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8, random_seed = 42)

ts
```

```{r}
#| echo: false
if (!file.exists("files/introgression/example.trees")) {
  ts_save(ts, file = "files/introgression/example.trees")
}
```

---

**We can extract a single tree at a given index using the function
`ts_tree()`.** (Note that because _slendr_ ties into the Python module _tskit_
behind the scenes, indexing into the tree sequence starts at 0.) **This doesn't
give us much information  though---it's just an opaque object in computer
memory, but we don't see anything interesting:**

```{r}
tree <- ts_tree(ts, i = 0)
tree
```

---

**We can use the built-in _slendr_ helper function `ts_draw()` to visualize
these tree objects. For instance, here's how we can visualize the 0-th (i.e.,
the first) tree in our small tree sequence. Note that by setting `labels =
TRUE`, we can see individuals' names at the tips of the tree (which are normally
only assigned numerical identifiers), as well as the fact that each individual
is represented by two tips (one for each of its chromosome).**

```{r}
ts_draw(tree, labels = TRUE, width = 1000, height = 500, title = paste("Tree #", tree$index))
```

---

**Take a few minutes visualizing different trees, perhaps starting from 0-th and
going forward, until you get bored!**

1. **As you do this, notice that "neighboring" trees tend to be quite similar (why do you think this is?).**

2. **Can you find an example of a tree which fits our underlying population tree
model?**

3. **How about trees which clearly "contradict" this model? Can you find any?**

4. **How about a tree which would show evidence of the gene flow from `p3`
to `px` we programmed in our model? Can you find one?**

5. **You might encounter red cross signs plotted on the trees---what do you
think these represent?**

**The outcome of an evolutionary simulation is completely random, so don't get
too frustrated if you don't find lots of meaningful information while doing
this.** At the very least, when you explore the trees along the tree sequence,
even for a small section of a genome like 1 Mb in this case, it makes you
appreciate just how complex real-world evolutionary processes are.

**If you want to explore the exact same tree-sequence that I had, you can load
it with the following commands and use it instead of your simulated data:**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to read my own tree sequence `ts` instead

```{r}
ts_path <- tempfile()
options(timeout = 600)
download.file("https://raw.githubusercontent.com/bodkan/simgen/refs/heads/main/files/introgression/example.trees", destfile = ts_path, mode = "wb")
ts <- ts_read(file = ts_path, model = model)
```

:::

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's what I found after a couple of minutes of visualizing different trees in
my tree sequence:

- **A neat and tidy genealogy which is completely concordant with our population
tree** (take a look at the tip labels with population names and compare this
tree to the overall population tree model we worked with in this chapter):

```{r}
i <- 203
tree <- ts_tree(ts, i)
ts_draw(tree, labels = TRUE, width = 1000, height = 500, title = paste("Tree #", tree$index))
```

We can also see that the tree immediately after this one is basically the same.
This is because of a single (ancient) recombination event which only affected
one branch in the tree, but the remainder of the genealogy stays the same
(because recombination didn't affect those individuals' ancestors):

```{r}
i <- 204
tree <- ts_tree(ts, i)
ts_draw(tree, labels = TRUE, width = 1000, height = 500, title = paste("Tree #", tree$index))
```

- **A tree showing a clear evidence of introgression from `p3` into `px`:**

```{r}
i <- 243
tree <- ts_tree(ts, i)
ts_draw(tree, labels = TRUE, width = 1000, height = 500, title = paste("Tree #", tree$index))
```

- **Another locus in the genome carries a tree which is an utter mess and
doesn't seem to be similar to our underlying population tree model at all:**

```{r}
i <- 114
tree <- ts_tree(ts, i)
ts_draw(tree, labels = TRUE, width = 1000, height = 500, title = paste("Tree #", tree$index))
```

Oh, and the red crosses represent mutations!

:::

I hope that this little exercise illustrates nicely just how much work
population genetic statistics do for us in understanding the hidden truth behind
real-world evolutionary processes---they do this by aggregating massive amounts
of convoluted data resulting from these genealogical processes, and help us
extract and see meaningful patterns in them.









## Bonus exercise (if you want a programming challenge)


When playing with $f$-statistics in this chapter, you've probably noticed
various symmetries in $f_4$ (but also other $f$-statistics) depending on the
arrangement of their "configuration" (order of populations). As a trivial
example, an $f_3(A; B, C)$ and $f_3(A; C, B)$ will give you exactly the same
value.

**Try to figure out how many unique $f_4$ values involving a single quartet (for
instance, quartets involving different permutations of p1, p2, p3, and p4
populations) are there. How about how many absolute values? You could answer
this by drawing and doodling on paper, but try to use computer simulations to do
this too! You can program whatever demographic model you'd like for this
purpose---the specifics don't matter much as long as the model has some four
populations involved.**

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" icon=false}
### Click to see the solution

Here's a complete script with comments explaining the most important steps:

```{r}
#| message: false
library(purrr)
library(dplyr)

library(slendr)
init_env()

p4 <- population("p4", time = 20000, N = 1000)
p3 <- population("p3", time = 6000, N = 1000, parent = p4)
p2 <- population("p2", time = 2000, N = 1000, parent = p3)
p1 <- population("p1", time = 1000, N = 1000, parent = p2)

model <- compile_model(populations = list(p1, p2, p3, p4), generation_time = 1)

ts <-
  msprime(model, sequence_length = 1e6, recombination_rate = 1e-8) %>%
  ts_mutate(mutation_rate = 1e-8)

# install a combinatorics R package:
# install.packages("combinat")
library(combinat)

# these are the four samples we can create quartet combinations from:
quartet <- c("p1_1", "p2_1", "p3_1", "p4_1")

# this is how we can generate all permutations:
quartets <- permn(quartet)
quartets

# how many permutations there are in total?
#   4! = 4 * 3 * 2 * 1 = 24
factorial(4)

# we should therefore have 24 different quartet combinations of samples
length(quartets)

# loop across all quartets, computing the corresponding f4 statistic
all_f4 <-
  map_dfr(quartets, function(q) ts_f4(ts, q[1], q[2], q[3], q[4])) %>%
  arrange(abs(f4))

# print all f4 values
print(all_f4, n = Inf)

# narrow down the results to only unique f4 values
distinct(all_f4, f4, .keep_all = TRUE)

# narrow down the results to only unique absolute f4 values
distinct(all_f4, abs(f4), .keep_all = TRUE)
```

:::
